newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - French performance pinned on rates.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - French performance pinned on rates.

text.p: Recent outperformance of French bonds against Bunds is pinned on expectations of the Bank of France lowering its intervention rate, analysts said on Tuesday.
But further outperformance might prove difficult to maintain, they said.
With German interest rates still 15 basis points below French rates some analysts anticipate a cut in French rates could be announced after Thursday's regular monetary meeting.
"The French still have a bit of room to play with," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC Markets.
"It would seem to suggest a cut of five or 10 basis points without causing too many problems. The currency is strong and the bond market would seem to justify it," said King in London.
The French intervention rate has been at 3.15 percent since it was last cut in mid-December, while the German repo rate has been held at 3.0 percent since August.
Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, said any rate cut this week would depend on the strength of the currency.

"They will keep an eye on the French franc which has been doing quite well against the mark and is in a reasonable position," she said. "A rate cut is pretty much anticipated with full convergence now priced into Pibor (interest rate futures)."
Iain Lindsay, bond strategist at Credit Lyonnais in Paris, agreed. He said investors had begun buying longer maturities and were showing interest in the five-year area.
"We are seeing the beginnings of an equilibrium in the market at the very front of the curve and greater buying interest moving longer on the curve," said Lindsay.
But analysts did not rule out the possibility that the French central bank would keep rates on hold.
"They might actually choose to do nothing on the basis that they have come in for a lot of criticism with the two new appointments on the council," said Lindsay.
"To do nothing would be the most distinct statement they could make and to forego a cut on Thursday is actually not that costly in terms of its economic benefit."
Lindsay said there were plenty of technical reasons to justify French interest rates actually being lower than German rates.

"But the Bank of France will in no way invite trouble on the foreign exchange markets at this juncture," he said. "We are running shorter and shorter of time in terms of exploiting such an interest rate advantage, given that by January 1, 1999 everybody believes that French and German rates will be one and the same."
The yield of the 6.5 percent OAT due October 2006 was at a spread of 15 basis points through Bunds at 1239 GMT compared with eight basis points at the beginning of the year.
But analysts said it would be difficult for the spread to make significant further progress unless signs started coming through that the German economy was about pick up significantly.

"There is not much difference to pinpoint between the two economies," said HSBC's King, adding that although the German economy was not particularly strong, it was not as weak as recent German data suggested.

The cold weather was in part to blame for last weeks high German unemployment figures, he said. "As that unwinds we will find Germany isn't underperforming in the way people seem to think it is at the moment."
